content: Propionic acid, also known systematically as propanoic acid, is a naturally occurring carboxylic acid with the chemical formula CH3CH2COOH. In its pure form, it is a colorless, corrosive liquid with a strong, pungent odor. The anion CH3CH2COO−, along with the salts and esters derived from propionic acid, are referred to as propionates or propanoates. Propionic acid was first identified in 1844 by Johann Gottlieb, who discovered it as a degradation product of sugar. Over the following years, other chemists synthesized the same compound through different methods, though they did not initially recognize it as the same substance. In 1847, French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas confirmed that these acids were identical and named the compound propionic acid, derived from the Greek words protos (meaning first) and pion (meaning fat). This name reflects its status as the smallest carboxylic acid (H(CH2)nCOOH) to exhibit properties characteristic of fatty acids, such as forming an oily layer when salted out of water and producing a soapy potassium salt. The physical properties of propionic acid are intermediate between those of smaller carboxylic acids, such as formic and acetic acid, and larger fatty acids. It is miscible with water but can be separated from water by the addition of salt. In both its liquid and vapor states, propionic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers, which cause its vapor to deviate significantly from the ideal gas law. Chemically, propionic acid shares the general reactivity of carboxylic acids, allowing it to form derivatives such as amides, esters, anhydrides, and acid chlorides. It can also undergo alpha-halogenation in the presence of bromine and phosphorus tribromide (PBr3), a reaction known as the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction, yielding CH3CHBrCOOH. Industrially, propionic acid is primarily synthesized through the hydrocarboxylation of ethylene, using nickel carbonyl as a catalyst. It can also be produced via the aerobic oxidation of propionaldehyde in the presence of cobalt or manganese ions, a process that occurs efficiently at temperatures as low as 40–50°C. Historically, significant quantities of propionic acid were generated as a byproduct of acetic acid production. Currently, BASF is the largest global producer, with an annual production capacity of approximately 80 kilotons. Biologically, propionic acid is formed as propionyl-CoA during the metabolic breakdown of fatty acids with odd numbers of carbon atoms and certain amino acids. Bacteria from the genus Propionibacterium produce propionic acid as a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism. These bacteria are found in the stomachs of ruminants and in human sweat glands, contributing to the characteristic odors of Swiss cheese and sweat. Propionic acid is widely used as a preservative due to its ability to inhibit the growth of mold and certain bacteria. The majority of commercially produced propionic acid is utilized in this capacity, particularly in animal feed and human food products. In animal feed, it is applied either directly or as ammonium propionate, while in human foods, such as bread and baked goods, it is commonly used in the form of sodium or calcium propionate. It has also been employed in older antifungal foot powders. Beyond its preservative role, propionic acid serves as a chemical intermediate in the production of synthetic cellulose fibers, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals. Its esters are occasionally used as solvents or artificial flavoring agents. The primary hazard associated with propionic acid is its potential to cause chemical burns upon contact with the concentrated liquid. Propionic acid is readily metabolized in the body and does not bioaccumulate. However, a study by MacFabe and colleagues demonstrated that intraventricular infusions of propionic acid in rats induced reversible behaviors resembling those observed in autism, including hyperactivity, dystonia, turning, and retropulsion. These rats also exhibited caudate spiking and developed limbic kindled seizures over time. The study proposed that this model could provide valuable insights into autism and warrants further investigation. The metabolism of propionic acid begins with its conversion to propionyl-CoA, a common intermediate in the metabolism of carboxylic acids. However, due to its three-carbon structure, propionyl-CoA cannot directly enter beta-oxidation or the citric acid cycle. Instead, it undergoes carboxylation to D-methylmalonyl-CoA, isomerization to L-methylmalonyl-CoA, and subsequent rearrangement to succinyl-CoA via a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme. Succinyl-CoA is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle and can be readily integrated into cellular metabolism. In the genetic disorder propionic acidemia, propionate accumulates in the mitochondria as propionyl-CoA and its derivative methylcitrate, both of which inhibit the tricarboxylic acid cycle. This accumulation can act as a metabolic toxin in liver cells and may also affect astrocytic function, as propionate is metabolized oxidatively by glial cells. Propionic acidemia has been shown to alter neuronal and glial gene expression, potentially through effects on histone acetylation. In humans, the skin harbors a bacterial species known as Propionibacterium acnes, which derives its name from its ability to produce propionic acid. This bacterium resides primarily in the sebaceous glands and is a major contributor to the development of acne.
